1 Kings 1.summary: King David is old and stricken in years, and his servants find a young woman, Abishag the Shunammite, to cherish him and keep him warm, but the king knew her not (1 Kings 1:1–4). Adonijah the son of Haggith exalts himself, saying I will be king, and with Joab and Abiathar he holds a feast by En-rogel, but he does not invite Nathan, Zadok, Benaiah, or Solomon (1 Kings 1:5–10). Nathan tells Bathsheba to remind David that he swore Solomon would reign, and Nathan comes in to confirm it (1 Kings 1:11–27). David swears that Solomon shall reign and tells Zadok and Nathan to set Solomon on the king's mule, bring him to Gihon, and anoint him (1 Kings 1:28–40). Adonijah's guests hear the trumpet and the shout God save king Solomon and flee, and Adonijah takes hold of the horns of the altar (1 Kings 1:41–51). Solomon says if Adonijah shews himself a worthy man not an hair of him shall fall, but if wickedness is found in him he shall die, and sends him home (1 Kings 1:52–53).
1 Kings 1.whereWeAre: 1 Kings follows 2 Samuel, which ended with David's altar at Araunah's threshingfloor. The book opens with David very old and his son Adonijah trying to make himself king, until Nathan and Bathsheba move David to have Solomon anointed (1:1-53). Chapter 2 gives David's last words and Solomon's first acts as king.

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Old and cold, he swears to Bathsheba that Solomon shall reign and has him anointed (1:1,28-40).

keyFigures.name: Adonijah
keyFigures.role: Exalts himself as king, then holds the horns of the altar in fear (1:5-10,49-53).

keyFigures.name: Solomon
keyFigures.role: Anointed king at Gihon and spares Adonijah if he proves worthy (1:38-40,52-53).

keyFigures.name: Bathsheba
keyFigures.role: Reminds David of his oath (1:11-21).

keyFigures.name: Nathan
keyFigures.role: Tells Bathsheba what to say and confirms it before the king (1:11-27).

keyFigures.name: Zadok
keyFigures.role: The priest who takes the horn of oil and anoints Solomon (1:39).

keyThemes.explanation: Adonijah makes himself king without asking his father, and invites only some of the court (1:5-10).
Solomon rides David's mule to Gihon and is anointed, and the people shout God save king Solomon (1:32-40).
Solomon says Adonijah will live if he is a worthy man, but will die if wickedness is found in him (1:50-53).

1 Kings 2.summary: David charges Solomon, saying I go the way of all the earth, be strong therefore, and shew thyself a man, and keep the charge of the LORD thy God (1 Kings 2:1–4). He tells Solomon not to let Joab's hoar head go down to the grave in peace for killing Abner and Amasa, to show kindness to the sons of Barzillai, and to deal with Shimei, who cursed him (1 Kings 2:5–9). David sleeps with his fathers after reigning forty years, and the kingdom is established in Solomon's hand (1 Kings 2:10–12). Adonijah asks Bathsheba to ask Solomon for Abishag, and Solomon says he might as well ask for the kingdom also, and sends Benaiah, who slays him (1 Kings 2:13–25). Solomon sends Abiathar to Anathoth, and when Joab flees to the horns of the altar, Benaiah slays him there, and Zadok and Benaiah take their places (1 Kings 2:26–35). Solomon makes Shimei build a house in Jerusalem and never cross the brook Kidron, and three years later Shimei goes to Gath, and Benaiah slays him, and the kingdom is established in the hand of Solomon (1 Kings 2:36–46).
1 Kings 2.whereWeAre: Chapter 1 ended with Solomon anointed and Adonijah sent home. Chapter 2 gives David's last words, his death after forty years, and Solomon's removal of Adonijah, Abiathar, Joab, and Shimei, so that the kingdom is established in his hand (2:1-46). Chapter 3 shows him asking for wisdom.

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Charges Solomon to keep the LORD's ways and to deal with Joab and Shimei, then dies (2:1-12).

keyFigures.name: Solomon
keyFigures.role: Has Adonijah, Joab, and Shimei put to death and removes Abiathar (2:19-46).

keyFigures.name: Adonijah
keyFigures.role: Asks for Abishag through Bathsheba and is slain (2:13-25).

keyFigures.name: Bathsheba
keyFigures.role: Brings Adonijah's request to Solomon (2:13-21).

keyFigures.name: Abiathar
keyFigures.role: Sent to Anathoth for backing Adonijah (2:26-27).

keyFigures.name: Joab
keyFigures.role: Flees to the altar and is slain there by Benaiah (2:28-34).

keyThemes.explanation: David tells Solomon to walk in his ways, that he may prosper in all that he does (2:1-4).
Adonijah's request for Abishag is taken as a new claim to the kingdom (2:13-25).
Joab, Abiathar, and Shimei are each dealt with, and the kingdom is established in Solomon's hand (2:26-46).

1 Kings 3.summary: Solomon makes affinity with Pharaoh king of Egypt and takes his daughter, and the people sacrifice in high places because no house was yet built to the name of the LORD (1 Kings 3:1–2). Solomon loves the LORD, walking in the statutes of David his father, and goes to Gibeon, the great high place, and offers a thousand burnt offerings (1 Kings 3:3–4). The LORD appears to him in a dream and says Ask what I shall give thee, and Solomon says I am but a little child, and asks for an understanding heart to judge thy people (1 Kings 3:5–9). The LORD is pleased that he did not ask for long life, riches, or the life of his enemies, and gives him a wise and an understanding heart, and riches and honour besides (1 Kings 3:10–15). Two harlots come before the king, each claiming the living child, and Solomon says Bring me a sword and divide the living child in two, and the true mother says give her the living child, and in no wise slay it (1 Kings 3:16–27). All Israel hears and fears the king, for they see that the wisdom of God is in him (1 Kings 3:28).
1 Kings 3.whereWeAre: Chapter 2 ended with the kingdom established in Solomon's hand. Chapter 3 shows him marrying Pharaoh's daughter, asking the LORD at Gibeon for an understanding heart, and showing that wisdom in the case of the two women (3:1-28). Chapter 4 tells how he ruled.

keyFigures.name: Solomon
keyFigures.role: Asks for an understanding heart and judges between the two women (3:5-9,16-28).

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Appears in a dream and gives Solomon wisdom, riches, and honour (3:5,10-14).

keyFigures.name: Pharaoh's daughter
keyFigures.role: Solomon's wife, brought to the city of David until his buildings are done (3:1).

keyFigures.name: The two harlots
keyFigures.role: Come before the king with one living child (3:16-27).

keyThemes.explanation: Solomon does not ask for long life or riches, but for an understanding heart to judge God's people (3:5-12).
He asks for a sword, and the true mother is shown by her love for the child (3:16-27).
The people sacrificed in high places because no house was yet built for the name of the LORD (3:2-4).

explainedReferences.explanation: Same event: Solomon asking God for wisdom at Gibeon.

1 Kings 4.summary: The chapter lists Solomon's princes, including Azariah son of Zadok the priest, scribes, a recorder, Benaiah over the host, and Adoniram over the tribute (1 Kings 4:1–6). He has twelve officers over all Israel, each of whom provides food for the king and his household one month in the year (1 Kings 4:7–19). Judah and Israel are many as the sand which is by the sea, eating and drinking and making merry, and Solomon reigns over all kingdoms from the river unto the land of the Philistines and the border of Egypt (1 Kings 4:20–21). The daily provision for his table is thirty measures of fine flour, threescore measures of meal, ten fat oxen, twenty pasture oxen, and an hundred sheep, besides venison and fowl (1 Kings 4:22–28). Judah and Israel dwell safely, every man under his vine and under his fig tree, from Dan even to Beersheba (1 Kings 4:25). God gives Solomon wisdom and largeness of heart, so that he speaks three thousand proverbs and his songs are a thousand and five, and men of all nations come to hear his wisdom (1 Kings 4:29–34).
1 Kings 4.whereWeAre: Chapter 3 ended with all Israel fearing the king for his wisdom. Chapter 4 shows how he ruled: his officers, his twelve districts, a land at peace under vine and fig tree, and his fame for proverbs and songs (4:1-34). Chapter 5 turns to his plans for the temple.

keyFigures.name: Solomon
keyFigures.role: Rules from the river to Egypt and speaks three thousand proverbs (4:21,29-34).

keyFigures.name: The princes and officers
keyFigures.role: Azariah, Benaiah, Adoniram, and others who help him rule (4:1-6).

keyFigures.name: The twelve officers over Israel
keyFigures.role: Each provides food for the king one month of the year (4:7-19,27-28).

keyFigures.name: The people of Judah and Israel
keyFigures.role: Many as the sand by the sea, safe and glad (4:20,25).

keyThemes.explanation: Solomon has princes and twelve officers who supply the king's table month by month (4:1-19).
Every man dwells under his vine and under his fig tree (4:20-25).
God gives him largeness of heart, and kings send to hear his wisdom (4:29-34).

1 Kings 5.summary: Hiram king of Tyre, who had always loved David, sends his servants to Solomon (1 Kings 5:1). Solomon tells him David could not build a house for the LORD because of the wars about him, but now the LORD my God hath given me rest on every side, and he purposes to build an house for the name of the LORD (1 Kings 5:2–5). He asks Hiram to have cedar trees hewn out of Lebanon, for there is none among them that can skill to hew timber like the Sidonians (1 Kings 5:6). Hiram rejoices and says Blessed be the LORD this day, which hath given unto David a wise son, and he agrees to send cedar and fir by sea in floats (1 Kings 5:7–9). Solomon gives Hiram twenty thousand measures of wheat and twenty measures of pure oil year by year, and there is peace and a league between them (1 Kings 5:10–12). Solomon raises a levy of thirty thousand men, ten thousand a month in Lebanon, with seventy thousand that bear burdens and eighty thousand hewers in the mountains, and great stones are hewed for the foundation (1 Kings 5:13–18).
1 Kings 5.whereWeAre: Chapter 4 ended with Solomon's fame. Chapter 5 shows him sending to Hiram of Tyre for cedar to build the house of the LORD, and organizing the workers who will cut and carry the timber and stone (5:1-18). Chapter 6 tells how the temple is built.

keyFigures.name: Solomon
keyFigures.role: Asks Hiram for cedar and raises a levy of workers (5:2-6,13-18).

keyFigures.name: Hiram king of Tyre
keyFigures.role: Blesses the LORD, and sends cedar and fir for wheat and oil (5:1,7-12).

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Could not build the house because of the wars about him (5:3).

keyFigures.name: Adoniram
keyFigures.role: Set over the levy of thirty thousand men (5:14).

keyFigures.name: The workers
keyFigures.role: Thirty thousand in shifts, seventy thousand burden bearers, eighty thousand hewers (5:13-16).

keyThemes.explanation: Solomon says the LORD has given him rest on every side, so he will build the house David could not (5:3-5).
Hiram sends cedar and fir, and Solomon sends wheat and oil, and there is peace between them (5:7-12).
Solomon raises a levy of thirty thousand men, and many more carry and hew (5:13-18).

1 Kings 6.summary: In the four hundred and eightieth year after the children of Israel came out of Egypt, in the fourth year of Solomon's reign, in the month Zif, he begins to build the house of the LORD (1 Kings 6:1). The house is threescore cubits long, twenty broad, and thirty high, with a porch, windows of narrow lights, and chambers round about (1 Kings 6:2–10). The stone is made ready before it is brought, so that there is neither hammer nor axe nor any tool of iron heard in the house while it is in building (1 Kings 6:7). The word of the LORD comes to Solomon, saying if he walks in his statutes, he will perform his word with David and dwell among the children of Israel (1 Kings 6:11–13). The inside is covered with cedar carved with gourds and open flowers and overlaid with gold, and in the oracle he sets two cherubims of olive tree ten cubits high (1 Kings 6:14–36). The foundation is laid in the fourth year and the house is finished in the eleventh year, in the month Bul, so that he is seven years in building it (1 Kings 6:37–38).
1 Kings 6.whereWeAre: Chapter 5 ended with the stones being hewed for the foundation. Chapter 6 tells how Solomon builds the temple over seven years, with a word from the LORD in the middle saying that he will dwell among his people if Solomon keeps his statutes (6:1-38). Chapter 7 describes his palace and the temple's bronze work.

keyFigures.name: Solomon
keyFigures.role: Builds the house of the LORD in seven years (6:1,14,37-38).

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Tells Solomon that he will dwell among Israel if they walk in his statutes (6:11-13).

keyFigures.name: The builders
keyFigures.role: Prepare the stone at the quarry so that no hammer is heard in the house (6:7).

keyThemes.explanation: The temple has a porch, a main room, and the oracle, with cherubims overlaid with gold (6:2-3,19-28).

keyThemes.theme: Obedience matters more than the building
keyThemes.explanation: The LORD tells Solomon he will dwell among Israel if they keep his statutes (6:11-13).
The house is begun in Zif and finished in Bul seven years later (6:37-38).

explainedReferences.explanation: Same event: Solomon building the temple, with different selections of details.

1 Kings 7.summary: Solomon builds his own house for thirteen years, with the house of the forest of Lebanon, a porch of pillars, a porch for the throne where he may judge, and a house for Pharaoh's daughter (1 Kings 7:1–12). King Solomon sends and brings Hiram out of Tyre, a widow's son of the tribe of Naphtali, filled with wisdom and understanding to work all works in brass (1 Kings 7:13–14). Hiram casts two pillars of brass, each eighteen cubits high, and names them Jachin and Boaz (1 Kings 7:15–22). He makes a molten sea ten cubits across standing on twelve oxen, ten bases of brass, and ten lavers (1 Kings 7:23–39). Hiram makes the pots, shovels, and basons, casting them in the plain of Jordan in the clay ground between Succoth and Zarthan, and Solomon does not weigh the brass because there are so many vessels (1 Kings 7:40–47). Solomon makes the golden altar, the table for the shewbread, and the candlesticks, and brings in the things David his father had dedicated (1 Kings 7:48–51).
1 Kings 7.whereWeAre: Chapter 6 ended with the temple finished. Chapter 7 tells of Solomon's thirteen years building his own houses, and of Hiram of Tyre casting the bronze pillars, the sea, and the other bronze furnishings for the temple (7:1-51). Chapter 8 tells how the ark is brought in.

keyFigures.name: Solomon
keyFigures.role: Builds his palace for thirteen years and has the temple furnished (7:1-12,48-51).

keyFigures.name: Hiram of Tyre
keyFigures.role: A widow's son filled with wisdom, who casts the brass work (7:13-47).

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: His dedicated silver, gold, and vessels are put in the temple treasury (7:51).

keyThemes.explanation: Solomon spends thirteen years on his own houses, the forest of Lebanon, the throne porch, and Pharaoh's daughter's house (7:1-12).
Hiram makes the pillars Jachin and Boaz, the molten sea, and the lavers (7:13-39).
David's dedicated treasures go into the house of the LORD (7:51).

1 Kings 8.summary: Solomon assembles the elders of Israel at Jerusalem to bring the ark of the covenant of the LORD up out of the city of David, in the feast in the month Ethanim, and the priests bring it into the oracle under the wings of the cherubims (1 Kings 8:1–9). When the priests come out, the cloud fills the house of the LORD, so that they cannot stand to minister, for the glory of the LORD had filled the house (1 Kings 8:10–11). Solomon blesses the congregation, saying Blessed be the LORD God of Israel, and prays LORD God of Israel, there is no God like thee (1 Kings 8:12–26). He asks But will God indeed dwell on the earth, since the heaven and heaven of heavens cannot contain thee, and asks him to hear in heaven his dwelling place (1 Kings 8:27–30). He asks the LORD to hear when a man trespasses, when Israel is smitten by enemies, when there is no rain, famine, or pestilence, when a stranger prays toward this house, and when they sin and are carried away captive (1 Kings 8:31–53). Solomon blesses the people, saying Let your heart therefore be perfect with the LORD our God, and offers twenty and two thousand oxen and an hundred and twenty thousand sheep, and keeps the feast fourteen days (1 Kings 8:54–66).
1 Kings 8.whereWeAre: Chapter 7 ended with the temple furnished. Chapter 8 is the dedication: the ark is brought in, the glory of the LORD fills the house, Solomon prays, and the people keep a great feast (8:1-66). Chapter 9 gives the LORD's answer to him.

keyFigures.name: Solomon
keyFigures.role: Brings in the ark, blesses the people, and prays the long prayer (8:1-2,12-61).

keyFigures.name: The priests
keyFigures.role: Carry the ark into the oracle and come out when the cloud fills the house (8:3-11).

keyFigures.name: The elders and congregation of Israel
keyFigures.role: Gather at the feast of Ethanim and are blessed (8:1-2,55).

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: His glory fills the house, and he is asked to hear in heaven his dwelling place (8:10-11,30).

keyThemes.theme: God is near and yet too great for a house
keyThemes.explanation: The glory fills the house, yet Solomon says the heaven and heaven of heavens cannot contain him (8:10-11,27).
Solomon asks the LORD to hear sin, defeat, drought, famine, battle, and captivity when they pray toward this house (8:31-50).
He asks the LORD to hear the stranger that comes from a far country for his great name (8:41-43).
Solomon tells the people to let their heart be perfect with the LORD and keep his statutes (8:56-61).

explainedReferences.explanation: Same event: The ark entering the completed temple and God's glory filling it.
Same event: Solomon's prayer at the temple dedication.

1 Kings 9.summary: When Solomon has finished the house of the LORD and the king's house, the LORD appears to him the second time, as he appeared at Gibeon (1 Kings 9:1–2). He says I have heard thy prayer, I have hallowed this house, and mine eyes and mine heart shall be there perpetually (1 Kings 9:3). If Solomon walks before him as David did, he will establish his throne for ever, but if they turn away and serve other gods, he will cut off Israel out of the land and cast this house out of his sight (1 Kings 9:4–9). After twenty years Solomon gives Hiram twenty cities in Galilee, and Hiram does not like them and calls them the land of Cabul (1 Kings 9:10–14). Solomon raises a levy to build the house of the LORD, his own house, Millo, the wall of Jerusalem, Hazor, Megiddo, and Gezer, using the people left of the Amorites, Hittites, and others as bondservants, but he makes no bondmen of the children of Israel (1 Kings 9:15–23). He offers burnt offerings and peace offerings three times a year, and builds a navy at Eziongeber, and Hiram's shipmen bring gold from Ophir (1 Kings 9:24–28).
1 Kings 9.whereWeAre: Chapter 8 ended with the dedication feast. Chapter 9 gives the LORD's answer: he will keep David's throne if Solomon obeys, but will cast the house out of his sight if Israel serves other gods, and then follows Solomon's cities, labour, and ships (9:1-28). Chapter 10 tells of the queen of Sheba.

keyFigures.name: Solomon
keyFigures.role: Receives the LORD's second appearance, and builds cities and ships (9:1-9,15-28).

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Promises to keep David's throne if Solomon walks before him, and warns of cutting off Israel if they turn (9:3-9).

keyFigures.name: Hiram of Tyre
keyFigures.role: Does not like the twenty cities and sends gold and shipmen (9:11-14,26-28).

keyFigures.name: Pharaoh's daughter
keyFigures.role: Comes up from the city of David to her own house (9:24).

keyThemes.explanation: The LORD's promise to David's throne depends on Solomon walking as David did (9:4-5).
If Israel serves other gods, the LORD will cast the house out of his sight and men will ask why (9:6-9).
Solomon builds cities, uses non-Israelites as bondservants, and sends ships to Ophir (9:15-28).

1 Kings 10.summary: When the queen of Sheba hears of the fame of Solomon concerning the name of the LORD, she comes to prove him with hard questions, with camels bearing spices, gold, and precious stones (1 Kings 10:1–2). Solomon tells her all her questions, and when she sees his wisdom, his house, his table, and the ascent by which he goes up to the house of the LORD, there is no more spirit in her (1 Kings 10:3–5). She says It was a true report, and behold, the half was not told me, and Blessed be the LORD thy God, which delighted in thee, to set thee on the throne of Israel (1 Kings 10:6–9). She gives the king an hundred and twenty talents of gold and spices, and Solomon gives her all her desire (1 Kings 10:10–13). Solomon receives six hundred threescore and six talents of gold in one year, makes two hundred targets and three hundred shields of beaten gold, and a great throne of ivory overlaid with the best gold (1 Kings 10:14–20). All his drinking vessels are gold, for silver is nothing accounted of in the days of Solomon, and he exceeds all the kings of the earth for riches and wisdom (1 Kings 10:21–25). He gathers fourteen hundred chariots and twelve thousand horsemen and makes silver in Jerusalem as stones, and horses are brought out of Egypt (1 Kings 10:26–29).
1 Kings 10.whereWeAre: Chapter 9 ended with Solomon's ships and cities. Chapter 10 shows the queen of Sheba visiting him, praising the LORD for his wisdom, and then lists his gold, throne, chariots, and horses, which are the height of his wealth (10:1-29). Chapter 11 tells how it all begins to unravel.

keyFigures.name: The queen of Sheba
keyFigures.role: Comes with hard questions, sees Solomon's house, and blesses the LORD (10:1-10).

keyFigures.name: Solomon
keyFigures.role: Answers all her questions, gives her her desire, and grows richer than all kings (10:3,13-23).

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: The one the queen blesses for setting Solomon on the throne (10:9).

keyFigures.name: Hiram's navy
keyFigures.role: Brings gold and almug trees from Ophir (10:11).

keyFigures.name: The kings and merchants
keyFigures.role: Bring presents, spices, and horses to Solomon (10:15,24-29).

keyThemes.explanation: The queen says it was a true report, and the half was not told me (10:6-7).
Solomon makes shields and a throne of gold, and silver is nothing accounted of in his days (10:14-23).
He buys horses and chariots from Egypt and sells them to the kings of the Hittites and Syria (10:28-29).

explainedReferences.explanation: Same event: The queen of Sheba's visit to Solomon.

1 Kings 11.summary: King Solomon loves many strange women, together with the daughter of Pharaoh, women of the Moabites, Ammonites, Edomites, Zidonians, and Hittites, of whom the LORD had said Ye shall not go in to them (1 Kings 11:1–2). He has seven hundred wives, princesses, and three hundred concubines, and when he is old they turn away his heart after other gods, so that his heart is not perfect with the LORD (1 Kings 11:3–6). He builds a high place for Chemosh and for Molech in the hill before Jerusalem (1 Kings 11:7–8). The LORD is angry, since he had appeared to him twice, and says I will surely rend the kingdom from thee, but not in thy days, for David's sake, and he will leave one tribe (1 Kings 11:9–13). The LORD raises up adversaries, Hadad the Edomite and Rezon of Damascus, and Ahijah the Shilonite tears a new garment into twelve pieces and gives Jeroboam ten (1 Kings 11:14–31). Solomon seeks to kill Jeroboam, who flees to Shishak in Egypt, and Solomon reigns forty years in Jerusalem, sleeps with his fathers, and Rehoboam his son reigns (1 Kings 11:40–43).
1 Kings 11.whereWeAre: Chapter 10 ended with Solomon's riches and horses. Chapter 11 shows his foreign wives turning his heart to other gods, the LORD's word that the kingdom will be torn from his son, and the rise of Jeroboam, whom the prophet Ahijah names for ten tribes (11:1-43). Chapter 12 tells how the kingdom splits.

keyFigures.name: Solomon
keyFigures.role: Loves many strange women, builds high places for their gods, and is told the kingdom will be rent (11:1-13).

keyFigures.name: His wives
keyFigures.role: Seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines who turn away his heart (11:1-4).

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Is angry and says he will rend the kingdom, but leaves one tribe for David's sake (11:9-13).

keyFigures.name: Hadad and Rezon
keyFigures.role: Adversaries raised up against Solomon (11:14-25).

keyFigures.name: Ahijah the Shilonite
keyFigures.role: Tears a new garment into twelve pieces to give Jeroboam ten (11:29-39).

keyFigures.name: Jeroboam
keyFigures.role: Told he will have ten tribes, flees to Egypt (11:26-40).

keyThemes.explanation: Solomon's wives turn his heart after other gods when he is old (11:1-8).
The kingdom will be rent, but one tribe remains for David's sake and Jerusalem's (11:9-13).
Ahijah tears a new garment into twelve pieces to show Jeroboam gets ten tribes (11:29-39).

1 Kings 12.summary: Rehoboam goes to Shechem to be made king, and Jeroboam, called out of Egypt, and all Israel say Thy father made our yoke grievous, make thou lighter, and we will serve thee (1 Kings 12:1–4). The old men tell him if he will be a servant unto this people they will be his servants for ever, but the young men say My little finger shall be thicker than my father's loins, and my father chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions (1 Kings 12:5–15). Israel answers What portion have we in David, to your tents, O Israel, and only the tribe of Judah follows the house of David, and they make Jeroboam king (1 Kings 12:16–20). Rehoboam gathers an army, but Shemaiah the man of God says Ye shall not go up, nor fight against your brethren, for this thing is from me, and they hearken (1 Kings 12:21–24). Jeroboam fears the people will return to Rehoboam, so he makes two calves of gold and says It is too much for you to go up to Jerusalem, behold thy gods, O Israel, and sets them in Bethel and in Dan (1 Kings 12:25–30). He makes priests of the lowest of the people and sets a feast in the eighth month, and this thing became a sin (1 Kings 12:31–33).
1 Kings 12.whereWeAre: Chapter 11 ended with Solomon's death and Jeroboam in Egypt. Chapter 12 tells how Rehoboam answers Israel harshly, ten tribes leave him and make Jeroboam king, and Jeroboam sets up golden calves at Bethel and Dan so that his people will not go to Jerusalem (12:1-33). Chapter 13 tells of a man of God at Bethel.

keyFigures.name: Rehoboam
keyFigures.role: Rejects the old men's counsel and answers Israel harshly (12:6-15).

keyFigures.name: Jeroboam
keyFigures.role: Comes back from Egypt, is made king, and sets up golden calves at Bethel and Dan (12:2-3,20,25-33).

keyFigures.name: The old men and the young men
keyFigures.role: Give opposite advice to Rehoboam (12:6-11).

keyFigures.name: Israel
keyFigures.role: Say to your tents, O Israel, and leave the house of David (12:16-19).

keyFigures.name: Shemaiah the man of God
keyFigures.role: Tells Rehoboam not to fight against his brethren (12:22-24).

keyThemes.theme: A king who will not listen
keyThemes.explanation: Rehoboam turns from the old men's counsel and takes the young men's (12:6-15).
Israel says What portion have we in David, and only Judah stays with Rehoboam (12:16-20).
Jeroboam sets up calves, other priests, and a new feast, so his people will not go to Jerusalem (12:26-33).

explainedReferences.explanation: Same event: Rehoboam's refusal and the division of the kingdom.

1 Kings 13.summary: A man of God comes out of Judah to Bethel as Jeroboam stands by the altar to burn incense, and cries O altar, altar, a child shall be born unto the house of David, Josiah by name, and men's bones shall be burnt upon thee (1 Kings 13:1–2). The altar is rent and the ashes poured out, and when Jeroboam puts forth his hand and says Lay hold on him, his hand dries up, and the man of God prays and it is restored (1 Kings 13:3–6). Jeroboam asks him home for a reward, but the man says he was charged not to eat bread nor drink water in this place, nor turn again by the same way (1 Kings 13:7–10). An old prophet at Bethel follows him and says an angel told him to bring him back, but he lied unto him, and the man of God goes and eats (1 Kings 13:11–19). The word of the LORD comes against him for disobeying, and on his way a lion meets him by the way and slays him, and the ass and the lion stand by the body (1 Kings 13:20–25). The old prophet buries him in his own grave and says Alas, my brother, and Jeroboam returns not from his evil way, and this thing becomes sin unto the house of Jeroboam (1 Kings 13:26–34).
1 Kings 13.whereWeAre: Chapter 12 ended with Jeroboam's calves and priests at Bethel. Chapter 13 tells how a man of God from Judah speaks against Jeroboam's altar, but then disobeys the word given him and is killed, while Jeroboam goes on in his evil way (13:1-34). Chapter 14 tells how judgment comes to Jeroboam's house.

keyFigures.name: The man of God from Judah
keyFigures.role: Speaks against the altar, then eats at Bethel against his charge and is slain by a lion (13:1-10,18-24).

keyFigures.name: Jeroboam
keyFigures.role: Stretches out his hand, is healed, and does not turn from his evil way (13:4-6,33-34).

keyFigures.name: The old prophet of Bethel
keyFigures.role: Lies to the man of God, then buries him and mourns (13:11-32).

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Gives the sign at the altar and the word of judgment (13:2-5,20-22).

keyThemes.theme: The word of the LORD is true
keyThemes.explanation: The altar is rent as the man of God said (13:1-5).
The old prophet says an angel spoke to him, but the LORD had given a different charge (13:15-24).
Jeroboam returns not from his evil way and goes on making priests of the lowest people (13:33-34).

1 Kings 14.summary: Abijah the son of Jeroboam falls sick, and Jeroboam tells his wife to disguise herself and go to Ahijah the prophet at Shiloh with ten loaves, cracknels, and a cruse of honey (1 Kings 14:1–4). The LORD tells Ahijah she is coming, and he says Come in, thou wife of Jeroboam, why feignest thou thyself to be another, for I am sent to thee with heavy tidings (1 Kings 14:5–6). He says that Jeroboam has done evil above all that were before him, making other gods and casting the LORD behind his back, so the LORD will take away the remnant of his house as a man taketh away dung (1 Kings 14:7–11). When her feet enter the city, the child shall die, and all Israel shall mourn for him, because in him there is found some good thing toward the LORD God of Israel (1 Kings 14:12–18). Jeroboam reigns twenty and two years and Nadab his son reigns in his stead (1 Kings 14:19–20). Rehoboam reigns seventeen years in Jerusalem, and Judah builds high places, images, and groves on every high hill and under every green tree (1 Kings 14:21–24). In Rehoboam's fifth year Shishak king of Egypt takes the treasures of the house of the LORD and the shields of gold, and Rehoboam makes brasen shields in their place, and there is war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam all their days (1 Kings 14:25–31).
1 Kings 14.whereWeAre: Chapter 13 ended with Jeroboam's evil continuing. Chapter 14 tells how Ahijah foretells the end of Jeroboam's house and the death of his sick son, and how Judah under Rehoboam also does evil and is raided by Shishak of Egypt (14:1-31). Chapter 15 follows the kings who come next.

keyFigures.name: Jeroboam
keyFigures.role: Sends his wife in disguise to ask about his sick son (14:1-4).

keyFigures.name: Jeroboam's wife
keyFigures.role: Goes to Shiloh and hears the heavy tidings (14:4-6,17).

keyFigures.name: Ahijah the prophet
keyFigures.role: Old and blind, he knows her and tells of judgment on Jeroboam's house (14:4-16).

keyFigures.name: Abijah
keyFigures.role: Jeroboam's son, who dies and is mourned because some good thing is found in him (14:12-13,17-18).

keyFigures.name: Rehoboam
keyFigures.role: King of Judah, whose treasures are taken by Shishak (14:21-28).

keyFigures.name: Shishak
keyFigures.role: King of Egypt, who comes up against Jerusalem (14:25-26).

keyThemes.explanation: Ahijah says the LORD will cut off the house of Jeroboam because he made other gods and cast the LORD behind his back (14:7-16).

keyThemes.theme: A good thing in a sick boy
keyThemes.explanation: The child will be buried in peace because in him is found some good thing toward the LORD (14:12-13).
Under Rehoboam, Judah builds high places, images, and groves, and Shishak takes the temple treasures (14:22-28).

1 Kings 15.summary: Abijam reigns three years in Jerusalem and walks in all the sins of his father, but for David's sake the LORD gives him a lamp in Jerusalem (1 Kings 15:1–8). Asa reigns forty and one years, and does that which is right in the eyes of the LORD, as did David, taking away the sodomites and the idols, and he removes his mother Maachah from being queen because she made an idol in a grove, though the high places are not removed (1 Kings 15:9–15). Baasha king of Israel builds Ramah, and Asa takes the silver and gold from the treasures of the house of the LORD and sends it to Benhadad king of Syria, who breaks his league with Baasha and smites Ijon, Dan, and Abelbethmaachah (1 Kings 15:16–22). Asa takes away the stones of Ramah and builds Geba and Mizpah, and Jehoshaphat his son reigns after him (1 Kings 15:22–24). Nadab son of Jeroboam reigns two years in Israel, and Baasha conspires against him, smites him, and slays all the house of Jeroboam, according to the word of the LORD by Ahijah (1 Kings 15:25–30). Baasha reigns twenty and four years and walks in the way of Jeroboam (1 Kings 15:31–34).
1 Kings 15.whereWeAre: Chapter 14 ended with war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam. Chapter 15 now moves quickly between the two kingdoms: Abijam and Asa in Judah, Nadab and Baasha in Israel, with Asa doing right but paying Syria with temple silver, and Baasha ending the house of Jeroboam (15:1-34). Chapter 16 follows the kings of Israel.

keyFigures.name: Abijam
keyFigures.role: King of Judah, who walks in his father's sins (15:1-8).

keyFigures.name: Asa
keyFigures.role: King of Judah, who does right, removes idols, and pays Benhadad (15:9-24).

keyFigures.name: Maachah
keyFigures.role: Asa's mother, removed from being queen because of her idol (15:13).

keyFigures.name: Baasha
keyFigures.role: Conspires against Nadab, kills the house of Jeroboam, and walks in his way (15:27-34).

keyFigures.name: Nadab
keyFigures.role: Jeroboam's son, who reigns two years and is slain (15:25-28).

keyFigures.name: Benhadad king of Syria
keyFigures.role: Is paid by Asa to break his league with Baasha (15:18-20).

keyThemes.theme: A king who did right, but not all
keyThemes.explanation: Asa removes idols and his mother's idol, yet the high places remain (15:11-15).
Asa takes silver and gold from the house of the LORD to send to Benhadad (15:16-22).
Baasha kills Nadab and all the house of Jeroboam as Ahijah had said (15:27-30).

1 Kings 16.summary: The word of the LORD comes to Jehu the son of Hanani against Baasha, saying that because he walked in the way of Jeroboam, the LORD will take away the posterity of Baasha (1 Kings 16:1–7). Elah his son reigns two years in Tirzah, and Zimri, captain of half his chariots, slays him while he is drinking himself drunk and slays all the house of Baasha (1 Kings 16:8–14). Zimri reigns seven days in Tirzah, and the people make Omri king, and Zimri burns the king's house over him with fire and dies (1 Kings 16:15–20). Half the people follow Tibni and half follow Omri, and Omri prevails, and Tibni dies (1 Kings 16:21–22). Omri buys the hill Samaria of Shemer for two talents of silver and builds a city, and does worse than all that were before him (1 Kings 16:23–28). Ahab his son reigns twenty and two years and does evil above all that were before him, takes Jezebel the daughter of Ethbaal king of the Zidonians, and serves Baal, setting up an altar and a grove in Samaria (1 Kings 16:29–33). In his days Hiel the Bethelite builds Jericho, and loses Abiram his firstborn and Segub his youngest, according to the word of the LORD by Joshua (1 Kings 16:34).
1 Kings 16.whereWeAre: Chapter 15 ended with Baasha in Israel. Chapter 16 shows the kings of Israel falling one after another, from Elah and Zimri to Omri, who builds Samaria, and then Ahab, who marries Jezebel and sets up Baal worship in the capital (16:1-34). Chapter 17 introduces Elijah.

keyFigures.name: Jehu the son of Hanani
keyFigures.role: Brings the LORD's word against Baasha (16:1-4,7).

keyFigures.name: Elah
keyFigures.role: Baasha's son, slain by Zimri while drunk (16:8-10).

keyFigures.name: Zimri
keyFigures.role: Slays Elah and the house of Baasha, reigns seven days, and burns the king's house over himself (16:9-20).

keyFigures.name: Omri
keyFigures.role: Made king by the army, buys the hill of Samaria, and does worse than all before him (16:16-28).

keyFigures.name: Ahab
keyFigures.role: Marries Jezebel, serves Baal, and builds a house and altar for him in Samaria (16:29-33).

keyFigures.name: Jezebel
keyFigures.role: The daughter of Ethbaal king of the Zidonians, Ahab's wife (16:31).

keyThemes.explanation: Zimri kills Elah, and the people then make Omri king, and Zimri burns the palace (16:8-20).
Omri buys the hill Samaria for two talents of silver and builds a city (16:23-24).
Ahab marries Jezebel, builds an altar and a house for Baal, and does more to provoke the LORD than all before him (16:29-33).

1 Kings 17.summary: Elijah the Tishbite tells Ahab As the LORD God of Israel liveth, before whom I stand, there shall not be dew nor rain these years, but according to my word (1 Kings 17:1). The LORD sends him to hide by the brook Cherith, where the ravens bring him bread and flesh in the morning and in the evening, until the brook dries up (1 Kings 17:2–7). The LORD tells him to go to Zarephath, which belongs to Zidon, where a widow woman will feed him, and she says she has only an handful of meal in a barrel and a little oil in a cruse (1 Kings 17:8–12). Elijah says Fear not, make me a little cake first, for the barrel of meal shall not waste, neither shall the cruse of oil fail, until the LORD sendeth rain, and so it is (1 Kings 17:13–16). The widow's son falls sick and there is no breath left in him, and she says art thou come unto me to call my sin to remembrance and to slay my son (1 Kings 17:17–18). Elijah carries the child up to his loft, stretches himself upon him three times, and cries Let this child's soul come into him again, and the LORD hears him, and he says See, thy son liveth (1 Kings 17:19–23). The woman says Now by this I know that thou art a man of God, and that the word of the LORD in thy mouth is truth (1 Kings 17:24).
1 Kings 17.whereWeAre: Chapter 16 ended with Ahab and his Baal worship. Chapter 17 introduces Elijah, who tells Ahab it will not rain, is fed by ravens, and stays with a widow of Zarephath whose meal and oil do not run out and whose son is raised (17:1-24). Chapter 18 tells of the contest on Carmel.

keyFigures.name: Elijah
keyFigures.role: Announces the drought, is fed by ravens and a widow, and prays for her son (17:1-24).

keyFigures.name: Ahab
keyFigures.role: The king to whom Elijah says there will be no dew or rain (17:1).

keyFigures.name: The widow of Zarephath
keyFigures.role: Gives Elijah the last of her meal, and her meal and oil do not fail (17:8-16).

keyFigures.name: The widow's son
keyFigures.role: Falls sick and dies, and the LORD gives his soul back (17:17-23).

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Sends Elijah to the brook and to Zarephath and hears his prayer (17:2-4,8-9,22).

keyThemes.explanation: Ravens bring Elijah bread and flesh, then a widow's meal and oil do not fail (17:2-16).
A widow in Zidon, Jezebel's country, feeds the prophet from her last meal (17:9-15).
Elijah cries to the LORD three times and the child's soul comes into him again (17:19-23).

1 Kings 18.summary: In the third year the word of the LORD comes to Elijah, Go, shew thyself unto Ahab, and I will send rain, and the famine is sore in Samaria (1 Kings 18:1–2). Obadiah, who feared the LORD greatly and had hid an hundred prophets in two caves, meets Elijah and tells Ahab he is there (1 Kings 18:3–16). Ahab asks Art thou he that troubleth Israel, and Elijah says I have not troubled Israel, but thou, in that ye have forsaken the commandments of the LORD, and he calls Israel and the prophets of Baal to mount Carmel (1 Kings 18:17–20). Elijah says How long halt ye between two opinions, if the LORD be God, follow him, but the people answer him not a word (1 Kings 18:21–24). The prophets of Baal cry from morning until noon and cut themselves, and there is neither voice, nor any to answer (1 Kings 18:25–29). Elijah repairs the altar of the LORD, pours water on it, and prays, and the fire of the LORD falls and consumes the sacrifice, and the people say The LORD, he is the God (1 Kings 18:30–39). Elijah has the prophets of Baal slain at the brook Kishon, and after he prays seven times a little cloud like a man's hand rises out of the sea, and there is a great rain (1 Kings 18:40–46).
1 Kings 18.whereWeAre: Chapter 17 ended with the widow's faith in the word of the LORD. Chapter 18 is the contest on mount Carmel, where the LORD answers Elijah by fire, the people say The LORD, he is the God, the prophets of Baal are slain, and the drought ends with rain (18:1-46). Chapter 19 shows Elijah afraid.

keyFigures.name: Elijah
keyFigures.role: Calls Israel to choose, prays, and runs before Ahab's chariot to Jezreel (18:1-2,21-46).

keyFigures.name: Ahab
keyFigures.role: Calls Elijah the troubler of Israel and goes to Jezreel in his chariot (18:17,41-46).

keyFigures.name: Obadiah
keyFigures.role: Governor of Ahab's house, who had hid an hundred prophets (18:3-16).

keyFigures.name: The prophets of Baal
keyFigures.role: Four hundred and fifty, who cry out and cut themselves with no answer (18:19,25-29).

keyFigures.name: The people of Israel
keyFigures.role: Are silent, then say The LORD, he is the God (18:21,39).

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Answers by fire and sends rain (18:38,45).

keyThemes.theme: Choosing between the LORD and Baal
keyThemes.explanation: Elijah asks How long halt ye between two opinions (18:21-24).

keyThemes.theme: The God who answers by fire
keyThemes.explanation: The fire of the LORD falls and consumes the offering, and the people fall on their faces (18:36-39).
Elijah has them taken to the brook Kishon and slain, which the story reports (18:40).
A little cloud like a man's hand rises, and a great rain follows (18:41-46).

1 Kings 19.summary: Ahab tells Jezebel all that Elijah has done, and she sends a messenger to say So let the gods do to me, and more also, if I make not thy life as the life of one of them by tomorrow (1 Kings 19:1–2). Elijah goes for his life to Beersheba, goes a day's journey into the wilderness, sits under a juniper tree, and asks that he might die, saying I am not better than my fathers (1 Kings 19:3–4). An angel touches him and says Arise and eat, and he goes in the strength of that meat forty days and forty nights unto Horeb the mount of God (1 Kings 19:5–8). The LORD asks What doest thou here, Elijah, and he says he is jealous for the LORD, and I, even I only, am left (1 Kings 19:9–10). A great and strong wind, an earthquake, and a fire pass, but the LORD is not in them, and after the fire comes a still small voice (1 Kings 19:11–13). The LORD tells him to anoint Hazael king over Syria, Jehu king over Israel, and Elisha to be prophet in his room, and says he has left seven thousand in Israel which have not bowed unto Baal (1 Kings 19:14–18). Elijah casts his mantle upon Elisha, who is plowing with twelve yoke of oxen, and Elisha kills his oxen, follows Elijah, and ministers unto him (1 Kings 19:19–21).
1 Kings 19.whereWeAre: Chapter 18 ended with Elijah running before Ahab's chariot. Chapter 19 shows Elijah, afraid of Jezebel, running to the wilderness and Horeb, where the LORD speaks in a still small voice, tells him he is not alone, and gives him Elisha (19:1-21). Chapter 20 turns back to Ahab and Syria.

keyFigures.name: Elijah
keyFigures.role: Flees from Jezebel, asks to die, meets the LORD at Horeb, and calls Elisha (19:3-21).

keyFigures.name: Jezebel
keyFigures.role: Sends a messenger to say she will kill him by tomorrow (19:1-2).

keyFigures.name: The angel
keyFigures.role: Touches Elijah and tells him Arise and eat (19:5-7).

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Speaks in a still small voice and gives Elijah three tasks (19:9-18).

keyFigures.name: Elisha
keyFigures.role: A plowman who leaves his oxen and follows Elijah (19:16,19-21).

keyThemes.explanation: Elijah asks to die, and the angel gives him bread and water twice (19:3-8).
The LORD is not in the wind, the earthquake, or the fire, but in a still small voice (19:11-13).
The LORD says he has seven thousand who have not bowed to Baal (19:14-18).
Elisha leaves his oxen, burns the plow gear, and follows Elijah (19:19-21).

explainedReferences.explanation: Elijah's complaint about killed prophets and demolished altars.
Reply that seven thousand had not bowed to Baal.

1 Kings 20.summary: Benhadad king of Syria gathers his host with thirty and two kings and besieges Samaria, and sends to Ahab saying Thy silver and thy gold is mine, thy wives also and thy children (1 Kings 20:1–3). Ahab agrees, but when Benhadad says his servants will search the houses, Ahab and the elders refuse, and Ahab says Let not him that girdeth on his harness boast himself as he that putteth it off (1 Kings 20:4–11). A prophet tells Ahab the LORD will deliver the great multitude into his hand, that thou shalt know that I am the LORD, and two hundred and thirty-two young men with seven thousand Israelites go out and the Syrians flee (1 Kings 20:13–21). The next year the Syrians say Their gods are gods of the hills, so a man of God says the LORD will deliver them into Ahab's hand, and Israel slays an hundred thousand footmen in one day at Aphek (1 Kings 20:22–30). Benhadad's servants come in sackcloth with ropes on their heads, and Ahab says He is my brother and makes a covenant and lets him go (1 Kings 20:31–34). A prophet disguised with ashes on his face tells Ahab Thy life shall go for his life, and thy people for his people, because he let go a man the LORD appointed to utter destruction, and Ahab goes home heavy and displeased (1 Kings 20:35–43).
1 Kings 20.whereWeAre: Chapter 19 ended with Elisha following Elijah. Chapter 20 returns to Ahab and the war with Syria: the LORD gives Israel two victories, but Ahab lets Benhadad go and a prophet tells him it will cost his life (20:1-43). Chapter 21 tells of Naboth's vineyard.

keyFigures.name: Ahab
keyFigures.role: Defeats the Syrians twice, then spares Benhadad and makes a covenant (20:13-21,29-34).

keyFigures.name: Benhadad king of Syria
keyFigures.role: Besieges Samaria, boasts, is defeated, and begs for his life (20:1-12,30-34).

keyFigures.name: The prophets
keyFigures.role: Promise victory in the LORD's name and later tell Ahab his life will go for Benhadad's (20:13,22,28,35-42).

keyFigures.name: The Syrian servants
keyFigures.role: Say the gods of Israel are gods of the hills (20:23-25).

keyThemes.explanation: The LORD gives Israel the Syrian host so that Ahab will know the LORD (20:13-21).
The Syrians say the LORD is God of the hills, but not of the valleys (20:23-28).
Ahab calls Benhadad his brother and lets him go, and a prophet judges him (20:31-43).

1 Kings 21.summary: Naboth the Jezreelite has a vineyard hard by the palace of Ahab, and Ahab asks for it for a garden of herbs, offering a better vineyard or its worth in money (1 Kings 21:1–2). Naboth says The LORD forbid it me, that I should give the inheritance of my fathers unto thee, and Ahab goes home heavy and displeased, lies on his bed, and will eat no bread (1 Kings 21:3–4). Jezebel says Dost thou now govern the kingdom of Israel, and writes letters in Ahab's name with his seal, telling the elders to proclaim a fast, set two sons of Belial before Naboth to say he blasphemed God and the king, and stone him (1 Kings 21:5–10). They do so, and Naboth is stoned and dead, and Jezebel tells Ahab to take possession of the vineyard (1 Kings 21:11–16). The word of the LORD comes to Elijah to meet Ahab in the vineyard, and Ahab says Hast thou found me, O mine enemy, and Elijah says I have found thee, because thou hast sold thyself to work evil (1 Kings 21:17–20). Elijah says dogs shall lick Ahab's blood and eat Jezebel by the wall of Jezreel (1 Kings 21:19–26). Ahab rends his clothes, puts on sackcloth, and goes softly, and the LORD says he will not bring the evil in his days, but in his son's days (1 Kings 21:27–29).
1 Kings 21.whereWeAre: Chapter 20 ended with Ahab heavy and displeased in Samaria. Chapter 21 tells how Ahab and Jezebel take Naboth's vineyard by false witnesses and murder, how Elijah announces judgment on them, and how Ahab humbles himself (21:1-29). Chapter 22 tells how Ahab dies.

keyFigures.name: Ahab
keyFigures.role: Wants Naboth's vineyard, sulks, takes it, and then humbles himself (21:1-4,15-16,27-29).

keyFigures.name: Naboth
keyFigures.role: Refuses to sell the inheritance of his fathers and is stoned (21:1-3,13-14).

keyFigures.name: Jezebel
keyFigures.role: Writes letters in Ahab's name and has Naboth killed by false witnesses (21:5-15).

keyFigures.name: Elijah
keyFigures.role: Meets Ahab in the vineyard and tells him judgment will come (21:17-24).

keyFigures.name: The elders and nobles
keyFigures.role: Carry out Jezebel's letters (21:8-13).

keyThemes.explanation: Naboth says The LORD forbid it me, that I should give the inheritance of my fathers (21:1-4).
Two false witnesses are set up to say Naboth blasphemed God and the king (21:8-14).

keyThemes.theme: The prophet says it to the king's face
keyThemes.explanation: Elijah says Hast thou killed, and also taken possession (21:17-24).
Ahab humbles himself, so the evil is put off to his son's days (21:27-29).

1 Kings 22.summary: After three years without war, Jehoshaphat king of Judah comes to Ahab, and Ahab asks him to go up with him to Ramothgilead, and Jehoshaphat says I am as thou art, but enquire at the word of the LORD (1 Kings 22:1–5). Four hundred prophets say Go up, for the LORD shall deliver it, but Jehoshaphat asks Is there not here a prophet of the LORD besides, and Ahab says there is Micaiah, but I hate him, for he doth not prophesy good concerning me, but evil (1 Kings 22:6–9). Zedekiah makes horns of iron, and Micaiah first says Go and prosper, then tells of Israel scattered as sheep that have not a shepherd (1 Kings 22:10–17). He says he saw the LORD on his throne, and a lying spirit was put in the mouth of all the prophets, and Ahab has Micaiah put in prison (1 Kings 22:18–28). Ahab disguises himself, and the Syrian captains are told to fight only with the king of Israel, and a certain man draws a bow at a venture and smites him between the joints of the harness, and he dies at even (1 Kings 22:29–37). They bury him in Samaria, and the dogs lick up his blood, and Ahaziah his son reigns (1 Kings 22:38–40). Jehoshaphat reigns twenty and five years and does right in the eyes of the LORD, though the high places are not taken away, and Ahaziah in Israel does evil and serves Baal (1 Kings 22:41–53).
1 Kings 22.whereWeAre: Chapter 21 ended with Ahab humbled but under judgment. Chapter 22 tells how Ahab and Jehoshaphat go to Ramothgilead, how four hundred prophets promise victory while Micaiah warns of death, and how Ahab is killed by an arrow shot at a venture (22:1-53). 2 Kings follows, with Ahaziah and Elijah.

keyFigures.name: Ahab
keyFigures.role: Plans the attack on Ramothgilead, disguises himself, and dies of an arrow (22:2-4,29-37).

keyFigures.name: Jehoshaphat
keyFigures.role: King of Judah, who asks for a prophet of the LORD (22:4-8,29-33).

keyFigures.name: Micaiah the son of Imlah
keyFigures.role: Tells the truth to the king and is put in prison (22:8,13-28).

keyFigures.name: The four hundred prophets and Zedekiah
keyFigures.role: Promise victory in the LORD's name (22:6,11-12,24).

keyFigures.name: Ahaziah
keyFigures.role: Ahab's son, who does evil like his father (22:40,51-53).

keyThemes.explanation: Four hundred prophets say Go up, but Micaiah says what the LORD says to him (22:5-28).
Ahab puts Micaiah in prison and dies at Ramothgilead as he had said (22:26-37).

keyThemes.theme: An alliance with a bad king
keyThemes.explanation: Jehoshaphat joins Ahab but asks first to enquire of the LORD (22:2-8,29-33).
Jehoshaphat reigns well in Judah and Ahaziah does evil in Israel (22:41-53).

explainedReferences.explanation: Same event: The campaign at Ramoth-gilead and Ahab's death.
